en: The Ritual for the Recitation of Mahāsukha-Vajrasattva, Extracted Briefly from the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*, the Supreme Yoga Tantra;
composed by [the monk] holding the rank of Kaifu Yitongsig, Tesheng, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Duke of Sushan.
I prostrate and pay homage to the Great Secret, who, arising from Vajradhara,
expounds the subtle and wondrous rituals; for those who practice the essential and true yoga,
may you give rise to a mind of benefit and joy.
Throughout the ten directions, without exception,
the realms of all sentient beings are accomplished through the nature of mantra; by reciting it according to one's will,
as soon as this thought arises, all obstacles are extinguished and removed.
Attaining peace, bliss, and joy, one transcends all Māras and becomes equal to the Tathāgatas;
honored by both the world and the gods,
one realizes that phenomena lack intrinsic nature and attains the ultimate bodhi.
Contemplating within one's own body the mind of Samantabhadra like the moon,
its physical form returns to empty stillness; from it emerges a five-pronged vajra,
pure white and radiant, which transforms into the likeness of a sattva.
Upon a simple lotus pedestal, adorned with the crowns of the five Buddhas, clad in crimson robes and backed by red light, you abide within perfect luminosity.
Therein reside the mantra and its respective mudrā; next, these are established.
The Benevolent One should sit in the half-lotus posture;
having cast the wheel of the wisdom-fist with the left leg pressing down upon the right, one should place it against the chest.
*Hūṃ* is the heart-mantra; the fist of meditative concentration is held arrogantly at the navel.
The vajra body, speech, and mind—do not let the limbs slant;
form the great mudrā of the deity. Next, bind the vajra-palms by joining the fingers upright and interlacing them at their first joints. Recite the mantra as follows:
VAJRA-JRĪM JRIṂ becomes the vajra-bind.
Its vidyā-mantra is as set forth below:
VAJRA-VAJRA-VANDHA VIKURVA HŪṂ PHAṬ. [This] opens the bind, destroys it, and strikes the heart.
One should recite the secret mantra as follows:
Next, with the previous vajra-bind, interlace the dhyāna and jñāna fingers between the tarjanī and madhyamā fingers while reciting the *Samantapraveśa* mantra;
may [the deity] descend and grant protection at every moment.
Without altering the preceding mudrā, add the powers of *dhyāna* (meditation) and *prajñā* (wisdom).
This is called the *samādhi-muṣṭi* (trance-fist). Recite the mantra in this manner;
divide that fist into two: the left in the *māna* (pride) position and the right at the heart.
The Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind: Regarding the physical form, follow the initial visualization;
as before, take the binding gesture as the standard.
With Wisdom and Effort like the gateways, Dhyāna presses within them. This is the secret samaya-mudrā.
At the heart, forehead, throat, and crown, one recites this mantra while forming the vajra-bind.
Furthermore, arranging the thumbs and ring fingers into the shape of a sword,
one presses the tips of the index and middle fingers against the side of the blade, according to the first [mudrā] of the first [chapter].
The dhyāna-seal rests upon the tip of wisdom;
as in the posture of the full lotus (*paryaṅka*), one should visualize it at the crown of the heart.
One should clearly imagine the Buddha Vairocana, solemn and radiantly white. Recite this mantra:
Next, one should seal the forehead; one should visualize Akṣobhya, blue in color, situated in front.
Reciting this secret mantra, one then places it upon the right side of the crown of the head; his name is the Honored One Ratnasaṃbhava.
With a yellow appearance, dignified and majestic, one recites the mantra in this manner and places it upon the crown of the head.
The Tathāgata Amitāyus has a particularly sublime crimson color; one invokes him by reciting this mantra.
Furthermore, at the crown of the head on the left is the green Amoghasiddhi, surrounded by the five Buddhas.
Reciting these secret mantra syllables, one next forms the jewel-garland mudrā; through this empowerment, the body is adorned.
Using the two Vajrapāṇis, one then winds [the garland] around the forehead;
again forming fists at the back of the head, one ties the wreath as before.
Slowly opening the *tanduhasta* and *prajñāhasta*, one lowers them to both sides like wings.
If one visualizes hanging silk ribbons, and during the recitation subsequently extends both the wings of Samādhi and Prajñā, clapping them together in unison, the mudrā is accomplished;
this pleases all the Honored Ones. The mantra is thus recited.
The mantra and mudrā of Vajramāna: silently recite it once in the heart, then again as above.
Adorned with the crown of Vajrasattva in the form of the five Buddhas, one abides in the samādhi-mudrā.
The Bhagavān Samantaprabha abides in the mudrā of the Tathāgata-fist;
next, one arranges the *acchupta* (brush) and forms a fist with the corner of the robe held in the samādhi-hand,
pressing it against the heart, while the wisdom-hand touches the earth according to the ritual.
The Wish-Fulfilling Gem is Ratnasambhava; the Wisdom Hand is held upward at the breast.
The Supreme Seal of Amitābha is the Samādhi Fist holding a lotus;
the Wisdom Fist resembles a blooming flower, just like that of Akṣobhya Buddha.
The mudrā of the Three Banners of Wisdom:
like one lifting up sentient beings, the hands are raised beside the breasts.
Furthermore, for the Amoghasiddhi mudrā, perform the vajra-bond, open the palms, and join the thumbs and ring fingers.
The *dāna* and *prajñā* [mudrās] are straight like mountain peaks;
the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* [mudrās] enter into the palms and join together like the shape of an arrow.
One should place these at the heart, forehead, throat, and crown of the head, and likewise apply them all with the secret mantras of the mind.
The Great Bliss Mind-Seal: Use it to bind and protect yourself with the preceding seal;
then, with the arrow piercing the heart, recite the subsequent mantra syllables so that all the Honored Ones may be pleased and the samaya is awakened.
Recite until reaching the syllable *Jwa* (弱), which clarifies that the *samaya* and *praṇidhāna* mudrās are like hooks;
having opened the hooks, the visualization of the mind is complete.
The Principal Deity descends to the ritual site, and the assembly of holy ones likewise arrives, remaining solemnly in their respective positions.
Patience and aspiration support one another; like a ringed rope, they form the syllable *hūṃ* as a noose to draw [the deity] in.
Twice entwined, they form a lock that brings all the holy ones to rest; the syllable *maṃ* is its vidyā-mantra.
Moving slowly up and down, the *pāṇa* forms the measure of a *droṇa*;
reciting its sound with clarity and resonance can delight the hearts of all the sages.
Then the *argha* mudrā is displayed: the hands remain firmly joined in the *vajra-pāṇi* gesture.
The *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* fingers are joined; the *vīrya* and *bala* fingers form a hook shape.
With the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* fingers, one pinches the base.
Forming the side-seal, one recites the syllable *Oṃ*, then lifts the fragrant water and recites the subsequent *argha* mantra.
Offer it near the forehead. According to the ritual, bathe the assembly of noble ones;
as before, visualize the full moon. Within the center of the altar, the Great Sage appears brilliant white;
abide in the samādhi of Vajragarva.
Furthermore, the four honored ones are described: the Eye-Arrow (Netraśara) is positioned in front;
his complexion is red and his garments are likewise.
He is adorned with a crown and a garland, and with two hands he draws a bow and arrow. His manner is one of gazing intently at the *sattva*.
The Honored One Keṭakrīla is white in color and resides to his right.
With both hands in the vajra-fist mudrā, he embraces the *samaya* consort behind him;
he is named "Love," and both his form and attire are blue.
With both fists raised, the wisdom arm is extended; the elbow is supported by the wings of meditative concentration as they together grasp the Makara banner.
On the left, known as Pride, the color is yellow; the fist rests at the hip, and the head is slightly tilted toward the left.
The Karman Seal Mantra: To empower and firmly establish the Great Holy Vajramada,
one should recite the heart-mantras of the deities in succession, beginning with the Eye-Arrow.
The two fists are each firmly clenched;
having completed the secret mudrā of the ritual for drawing the bow and releasing the arrow, recite the vidyā-mantra as follows,
while maintaining the previous mudrā with both hands joined at the chest.
Kṣitigarbha Bhagavān: After reciting this subsequent phrase, one should again change the preceding mudrā.
With the wisdom arm held straight like a banner and the samādhi fist resting upon the elbow, one recites the vidyā; this is called the Mudrā of Affection.
The two fists are each placed at the hips;
by tilting the head toward the left, the mudrā of slow engagement is formed.
Recite the mantra as follows, then present the inner offerings, beginning from the southeast corner.
Holding a flower, his form is white; Vajra-Subhaga is of a joyful nature.
Vajra-Gandhe is black in color and holds an incense burner;
Vajra-Cakṣu offers lamps and is red in color, adorned with ornaments.
The powder is for the stage of the unguent;
the form and substance of the Great Auspicious Vajra are entirely yellow. Next, arrange the mudrās:
both begin with the two fists in a dancing posture, and they are then formed according to the ritual procedure.
With two vajra-fists joined together, visualize scattering sublime flowers by tossing them upward as an offering;
recite the mantra as follows.
Then, with the universal fists, toss them downward while contemplating an ocean-like cloud of burning incense.
Pervading all things, recite the mantra as follows:
with the two fists joined, the thumbs and wisdom-fingers interlocked, one should visualize the movement like a lamp, extensively performing buddha-activities; thus one utters the secret mantra.
Cover both fists with the palms facing downward, rest them against the chest, and spread the fingers outward in the manner of an exquisite *vilepana* (scented unguent).
While reciting this mantra, perform external offerings to the deities; furthermore, visualize [the offerings] in the four corners.
In the southeast is named *He-he* (Joyful Play); with both fists placed at the heart, one smiles.
In the southwest is *Xiao-chu* (Abiding in Laughter); with both palms spread beside the mouth, one sings.
In the northwest is *Ge-ju* (Abiding in Song); one plays and holds the *konghou* lute.
The dance of the Northeast is named [as such]; its movements and forms are performed according to the ritual, with all garments being golden in color.
The mantra and mudrā are further displayed by placing both fists together, covering them, and rotating them to the right around the heart.
This is called the Seal of Joyful Play (*Ratimudrā*). Its mantra is as recited below;
[form] the seal as before at the side of the mouth.
With the hands in the *dharmajñāna* [mudrā], slowly open and raise the palms, extending the arms fully. Smiling, recite the mantra.
The arms are held steady like a *vīṇā* lute;
the fingers are slightly bent as if drawing the strings with the feathers of wisdom.
To sing its brilliance, the two fists dance at the heart; joining them at the crown of the head, they then disperse.
Its name is the Mudrā of the Dance; the mantra syllables are then set forth.
Four attendants dwell at the gates, their forms and appearances to be further described.
First, one holds a hook and is blue in color, standing resplendent within the space.
The southern *śūla* is entirely yellow; the western *pāśa* is reddish-brown.
That which is in the north is called the *ghaṇṭā*, green in color.
[These] constitute the secret mudrās and mantras. Furthermore, I shall now set them forth.
The backs of the two fists should be pressed together; the *tarjanī* and *sūci* fingers hook back-to-back while the *tarjanī* fingers are extended to their full length.
Then, slightly bending the *sūci* fingers and moving them forward with a subtle beckoning gesture constitutes the *ākarṣaṇa-mudrā*. Its mantra is as follows: [as recited below].
With the previous mudrā, the fingers of the advancing force (injili) are crossed and their tips pressed against each other, forming a ring-like noose in the center.
Reciting the subsequent mantra, advance and hook the fingers of the advancing force together; open the fists and cross the backs.
Thus it is named "The Accomplishment of the Lock-Seal. The secret mantra is recited as follows:
"Like the backs of two locks joined together, moving and vibrating;
this is the adornment of the Great Sage—the flowered seat and the robes."
Together with the other deities previously mentioned, their colors vary according to their physical characteristics and they possess various forms and manifold virtues;
with the crowns of the five Buddhas upon their heads,
they shall establish the maṇḍala— first, one should maintain the visualization of all these positions.
The lunar disk appears, perfectly round and luminous;
within it, one visualizes the half-face form of the deity.
With eyes filled with joy as one gazes upon it, one performs the samādhi mudrā as previously presented before the deity.
Those mudrās and mantras should be performed according to the ritual without error.
Next, one should establish the other deities; likewise, beginning with the Eye-Arrow, one should protect the body as previously described.
Then, perform the Mahāsukha-cittānupraveśa-mudrā.
Exerting the power of advancement to the utmost, first separate the backs so they touch, then press both the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* fingers together.
When the seal is properly aligned and accomplished, press the *dhyāna* finger upon the *prajñā* finger;
through deep interlocking, the mudrā is then perfected.
It is named Kīlikā; next, one displays the signs of Makara.
Advancing the hook toward the perfection of aspiration, with power one digs at the tip of wisdom.
Morality extends it into a needle, and when generosity and wisdom are joined, it becomes straight.
The dhyāna and wisdom [hands] face each other;
each presses upon the side of the *jin* and *riki* fingers, forming the seal of mutual embrace.
Without altering the previous mudrā, touch the thighs from the outside—first with the right, and likewise with the left.
The inner offerings are further clarified: holding the *vajra* in the palm and tossing it to the side constitutes the flower mudrā;
scattering it below forms the incense;
pressing together the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* fingers forms the lamp; and for the unguent, one opens [the hands] at the chest.
Perform the playful circumambulation prostration; with the seal of laughter, bring it near the mouth.
Slowly open the self-dāna-wisdom [seal], then form the seal of song by modifying the *pāramitā* [seal] so that the fingers are slightly bent.
Advance the empty [thumb] and flick it between them.
With concentration, perform *khaṭakā*; with wisdom, form three banners at the heart and then whirl in dance.
Having completed the eight offerings, again bind the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*) and slightly bend the legs in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.
Slowly summoning with this hook-seal, one should bind from the fetter;

between the powers of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the seal is formed as a ring-locked chain, advancing through the powers of meditative concentration and wisdom; having grasped it, they immediately hook together.
Furthermore, one forms the firm bond; with meditative concentration and wisdom, the girdle is lowered to the chest.
Then, shaking it, one performs the mantra for the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as the *samaya*.
It is the same as the previous *karma* verses.
In the station of Vajrasattva and wherever the practitioner resides,
there are sixteen deities surrounding [the central figure] in a majestic array;
they dwell as described in the subsequent praise of the King [of Mantras], which one should recite.
By means of this vajra song, great bliss, passion, delight, and joy shall all become firm;
one will attain the siddhi of one’s wishes.
Furthermore, recite the supreme praise of reality as it is set forth below.
Because one can achieve success simply by reciting [the name], it swiftly brings the *siddhi* to completion.
Next, the characteristics of the eye-mudrā are set forth:
starting with the Great Sage, each subsequent one has a distinct visual form, and their names are likewise distinguished.
Furthermore, the practitioner should gaze upon the Honored One,
the Great Delightful Vajra, with the Vajra Eye;
one should contemplate the limit of the *sattva* while employing the Seal of Amoghasaṃcodana and simultaneously giving rise to the mind of great passion.
Through the empowerment of this mudrā, one shall swiftly achieve accomplishment;
form the three-fold banner gesture with wisdom. As before, place the *dharmacakra* at the heart;
having finished the dance, assume the posture of scattering flowers.
With eyes half-closed and a smiling face, gazing up at the Great Delightful Vajra,
the Lord of Beings; with the mudrā of the Unfailing Arrow and the Wisdom of the Essential Nature of the Dharmadhātu—
by means of these, one is able to abide [in the state].
Greatly pleasing to behold is the form of the Honored One, the Noble One;
with a gaze of great delight, she holds the mudrā. Even those of little merit shall swiftly fulfill their aspirations;
look upon me with a gracious countenance and grant the great accomplishment through your empowerment.
Furthermore, one should cause him to realize directly: The Great Joy Vajra,
who transcends the followers of external paths, Adorned with banners and victory standards,
and marked by the seal, Lifting his eyes and gazing slowly about, He shall certainly perform the *khaṭaka* [gesture].
Prajñā should bind three banners; as before, she performs the gesture of whirling dance and also the posture of casting flowers.
Her name is the Seal of Prostration, which brings about the homage of all humans and devas throughout the three realms; one should offer worship to her with reverence.
Next, perform the five types of gazing as before;
for the mantra of the deity, recite the syllable HŪṂ, the vidyā-mantra, and the pride of the mudrā.
For all others, recite the phrases of the *karma-mudrās*; they are no different from what was previously described.
The body accomplished by the Great Sage is the wisdom of the essential nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
As before, he gazes with passionate attachment;
furthermore, he causes [beings] to behold *parinirvāṇa* by slightly opening his eyes, causing his eyelashes to quiver.
That is called "Clear Vision. By means of this, one invites the Honored One to enter pervasively into one's own body.
With a mind of affectionate devotion, one serves the Noble One;
through the power of the mudrā, one accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Having realized the nature of wisdom, the *sattva* dwells therein;
now practicing this skillful means, I shall realize accomplishment.
Having performed the offerings according to the instructions, one next employs the mudrā for expulsion.
The Vajra Blazing Sun is named by the samaya;
with the two hands joined palm-to-palm, the eight fingers interlaced, the thumbs and little fingers extended,
and the faces of the wisdom-fingers joined like a vajra, it is the "empty fist."
Turning to the left can dispel māras; Circling to the right, one completely binds the boundary.
With the sound of *hūṃ* like a thunderclap, Act according to your will as a protective fence.
Contemplate with self-conquest and resolve Throughout the entirety of the realm of space.
Scented unguents, lamps, food, and drink;
flower garlands, incense, clothing, parasols, banners, and streamers;
fans, fly-whisks, songs, precious bells, exquisite dances, and palaces—this is the ritual for supreme offerings.
I now manifest through transformation so that all the noble ones may enjoy it;
as before, recite the syllable Oṃ while visualizing it,
with an unblinking gaze and a smiling countenance, with a mind of firm and joyful devotion.
Having long contemplated the essence of the Sage,
the Vajra-eye is then perfected as the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) of the Vidyādhara. In the Sattvasamādhi,
the lips and teeth should be kept together, and the Vajra-speech is free from sound.
Without moving the tip of the tongue much, one can accomplish all the teachings.
Just as one wishes to bring [the recitation] to rest, one should again visualize the ritual of offering and recite the *oṃ* mantra; as before, one should present it.
The One Hundred and Eight Names of Praise: Next, one should recite them.
If one maintains this King of Praises, the Vajra Dharma-speech, whatever one desires shall be accomplished swiftly and beyond compare.
Each day, one should promptly recite: "I have departed from all sins;
May I be forever freed from all suffering; The Pure Land shall manifest before me;
By merely reciting this, all merits are perfected, Increasing auspiciousness and radiant splendor."
Next, present the arghya mudrā: place the side of the seal at the edge of the vessel and incline it accordingly;
while visualizing the prostration and reciting the syllable *Oṃ*, offer it according to the ritual rules and chant its root mantra.
Having completed the making of the vow, bind the previous [boundary].
Visualize the blazing vajra-sun rotating counter-clockwise to dissolve the boundary.
Then, form the firm vajra-bind mudrā by extending the *kṣānti* and *varaṇa* fingers upward like needles; recite the mantra at the heart:
When the recitation ends, bring [the visualization] near the forehead;
from the point of the blade, slowly open [the visualization] while imagining the assembly of sages returning to their palaces. To protect oneself, follow wherever one goes.
For those who wish to practice in advance, they should remain at the site of practice throughout the four seasons.
Recite until one *lakṣa* is completed; thereafter, maintain the recitation day and night, for the various deities shall provide protection.
Furthermore, apply yourself with diligence to the gateway of recitation and practice it throughout the four modes of conduct.
Just as previously vowed to deliver, one should also recite the words first spoken for all sentient beings in the realm without exception;
furthermore, one should invoke the secret mantra of bodhicitta by pronouncing the syllable *A*, using words that are wondrous and pleasing.
Realizing that all phenomena are unborn, one should clearly and attentively contemplate the five-pronged vajra,
as brilliant and perfect as the initial dwelling in the contemplation of emptiness,
and achieve the identity of one’s own body with the true form of the *sattva*. Contemplate this with vivid clarity.
Sitting in the half-lotus posture with the right leg pressing upon the left, join the vajra palms to form the firm and solid bond (*vajrabandha*).
Next, perform the mudrā for entering the heart universally;
the *samādhi-muṣṭi* is likewise formed. Then, rotate the *vajramāna-mudrā*.
Visualize the crown adorned with the five Buddha-seal jewels, with flower garlands tied and ribbons hanging in alternating lengths;
clap the hands together to maintain the samādhi-mudrā,
and with this seal, invite the Honored One to descend into one’s own body.
The eight clouds of offerings assemble;
as previously established, they all rely upon the great emptiness.
Having clearly visualized their arrangement and arrayed them, one presents the mudrā of vajra-pride.
For all other offerings to the Honored One, one employs the *karmamudrā*;
here, only the names of the seals are indicated. Their forms are as previously explained;
one should recite the respective root mantras while simultaneously performing mental offerings.
Having contemplated that the form of the body is empty, this is truly beholding the Honored One.
For those sentient beings who possess such superior resolve and are free from doubt and hesitation regarding these causes and conditions,
they realize that all is fundamentally empty.
Furthermore, establish the ritual of equal veneration;
thus abiding in yoga, whenever encountering any adorned object—whether pleasing, extraordinary, or flowing—contemplate them all as empty.
Next, re-establish [the visualization].
Once all have been rendered pure, visualize making offerings to the *iṣṭadevatā* while reciting the mantra of the syllable Oṃ;
partake of the enjoyments as Samantabhadra and perform the preliminary rites, practicing them wherever one may be.
When the count reaches one lakṣa, reciting as before day and night—
if one practices with single-minded diligence for one month, two months, or even half a month—
the deity will appear before one; then, according to one's wish, one shall seek accomplishment.
Delight in ascending to the rank of a Buddha-seed;
once faith in the Bodhisattva and the Deity is established, one’s very body becomes that [deity].
Even for those with heavy obscurations or who are indolent, upon reaching such certainty, they shall swiftly attain realization in this very life.
The Gate of Subtle Great Bliss:
A Brief Extract from the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*, the Supreme First Yoga Tantra, Entitled the Ritual Manual for the Recitation of Mahāsukha-vajrasattva; it should be venerated by the benevolent.
